lesson.title: From Photon to Fuel: How the Light Reactions Build ATP and NADPH
lesson.summary: The light dependent reactions link Photosystem II and Photosystem I through an electron transport chain that builds a proton gradient and reduces NADP+, converting captured light energy into ATP and NADPH.
lesson.body:
The light dependent reactions are the thylakoid membrane's answer to a specific problem: how to convert the fleeting energy of an excited electron, produced the instant a photosystem absorbs light, into stable, storable chemical energy the cell can use elsewhere. They accomplish this by linking Photosystem II and Photosystem I together through an electron transport chain, a sequence of redox reactions in which each carrier molecule is reduced by picking up the traveling electron and then oxidized as it passes that electron to the next carrier in line.

The pathway, often called linear electron flow, begins when light strikes Photosystem II and boosts an electron from its P680 reaction center to a primary acceptor. That electron then passes through a mobile carrier called plastoquinone, then the cytochrome b6f protein complex, then a small mobile protein called plastocyanin, before finally arriving at Photosystem I's P700 reaction center, restoring the electron that center lost when it, too, absorbed a photon. Every one of these handoffs is a redox reaction: the carrier receiving the electron is reduced, and the carrier releasing it is oxidized, exactly like the coupled oxidation reduction reactions found throughout cellular metabolism.

As electrons pass through the cytochrome b6f complex specifically, the energy released by that redox reaction is used to actively pump protons from the stroma into the thylakoid lumen, building up a proton concentration gradient across the thylakoid membrane. This same membrane compartment is also gaining protons directly from the splitting of water at Photosystem II, so the lumen becomes increasingly proton rich as electron flow continues. That gradient, and how the cell uses it to make ATP, is developed fully in the electron transport chain concept that follows this one.

Once the electron reaches Photosystem I's reaction center, a second photon absorption there boosts it to an even higher energy level, from which it is passed to a small iron sulfur protein called ferredoxin and finally to the enzyme NADP+ reductase, which uses it, along with a proton, to reduce NADP+ into NADPH. This reaction stores chemical energy and reducing power in a form the Calvin cycle can use directly to help build sugar, making NADPH one of the two essential outputs of the light dependent reactions, alongside the ATP generated by the proton gradient.

Some electrons take a shorter path called cyclic electron flow, cycling from Photosystem I back through part of the electron transport chain and back to Photosystem I again instead of continuing on to NADP+ reductase, which generates extra ATP without producing NADPH whenever the cell's ratio of these two products needs adjusting. Either way, the light dependent reactions convert the raw energy of sunlight, captured initially at the photosystems, into the ATP and NADPH that will power carbon fixation, while the two topics still to be detailed, water splitting and the full electron transport chain, fill in exactly how the electron supply and the proton gradient are generated.
